newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Aid workers quit Zairean city, cite security.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers quit Zairean city, cite security.

text.p: Foreign aid workers left Zaire's third city of Kisangani on Saturday, citing insecurity and reporting the retreat of Zairean troops and Rwandan Hutu militia allies before advancing Tutsi-led rebels.

"They were retreating from the direction of Amisi further east. They started arriving yesterday morning," one aid worker who was in Tingi Tingi refugee camp on Friday told Reuters after arriving in the capital Kinshasa.

Another aid worker said Serb mercenaries outside Kisangani turned back a relief convoy trying to leave for Tingi Tingi, the largest refugee camp left in eastern Zaire and make-shift home to an estimated 170,000 Hutu refugees.
"The Serb mercenaries shot in the air to turn back the convoy on Friday morning," he said.

The aid workers said Hutu refugees, many of whom fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals after the genocide there of minority Tutsis by hardline Hutus, had started leaving Tingi Tingi 200 km (125 miles) south of Kisangani.
They said Kisangani, on the Zaire River and headquarters for army operations in the war zone, was calm on Saturday.

Zaire's defence ministry said government troops still controlled Kindu, a regional transport hub and army operational base further south, but independent sources said the town appeared to have fallen to rebels on Friday afternoon.
Hubert Edongo, Kinshasa representative of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said 57 relief workers from the U.N. and non-governmental organisations were leaving Kisangani.
"Since we were proving unable to work and had no security guarantees in an operational zone, it was decided to withdraw our staff temporarily to Kinshasa," he told Reuters.
"The other element, and it's extremely important, is the suspension of safe conduct permits which have been blocked since the beginning of the week," he said.

The rebels, who took up arms in October and hold towns and territory in the east, responded to a January 20 army counter-offensive by attacking on several fronts, throwing the notoriously ill-disciplined army on the defensive.
The rebels say they have captured Kindu, up-river from Kisangani. Defence officials hotly deny this, saying extra troops went in on Friday with the regional commander.
"General Kalume Numbi landed at Kindu yesterday," one said on Saturday. "We are sending further reinforcements in today."
Kindu is about 400 km (250 miles) south of Kisangani, which the rebels have identified as a target.
"The security situation at Kindu does not permit us to deliver aid," Edongo said.
"At Tingi Tingi extreme tension has meant that our staff have had to leave in the past few days," he added.
Witnesses say armed Hutu hardliners were among the refugees, who include Burundian Hutus. Aid workers say up to 40 refugees are dying a day from hunger and disease.

Zaire accuses neighbouring Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of invading in support of the rebels. It has rejected direct peace talks with the rebels, something South Africa's President Nelson Mandela has been trying to organise.

It says it is prepared to join regional peace talks in Nairobi, once all foreign troops have left its territory, and an Organisation of African Unity summit in Togo on March 26 on the crisis in Central Africa's volatile Great Lakes region.
